analysis.one_liner: Strips federal Clean Water Act protection from many streams, wetlands, and ditches.
analysis.headline: A bill to narrow which waters the Clean Water Act covers, backed by just one Republican cosponsor, died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the 2015 Waters of the United States rule, which defined which streams, wetlands, and other waters are protected under the Clean Water Act. It would rewrite the law so that federal protection covers mainly year-round waters that flow into interstate waters, and explicitly excludes intermittent streams, groundwater, man-made ditches and irrigation systems, and most wetlands without a visible surface connection. It would also create a fast, binding process for landowners to get a determination that a water on their property is not federally protected. Fewer protected waters means fewer federal permits and pollution limits for farming, construction, and industrial discharges.
analysis.who_benefits: Landowners and businesses that discharge into or build near smaller streams and wetlands: farms with drainage ditches and prior-converted cropland, real estate developers, and energy or mining operations using ephemeral streams. They would face fewer federal permit requirements and pollution restrictions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farms, developers, and energy or mining firms

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the EPA's 2015 Clean Water Rule (the Waters of the United States rule) outright and replaces the statutory definition of protected waters with a much narrower one [S2] [S3].

Explicitly excludes intermittent and ephemeral streams, groundwater, man-made ditches and irrigation or drainage systems, prior converted cropland, and waste management systems from federal jurisdiction [S3].

Lets any landowner or permit applicant request a binding, expedited federal determination that a water is not protected; if the Army Corps does not answer within 60 days, the water is deemed not protected, and that finding is binding indefinitely while the person owns the property [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People downstream: communities whose drinking water comes from streams the bill would leave unprotected, and the public more broadly, since pollution discharged into excluded streams, ditches, and wetlands would no longer face federal Clean Water Act limits and could degrade larger rivers and lakes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Downstream communities and public water users

drawbacks.text: Intermittent and ephemeral streams, which the bill excludes, carry flows and pollution into the permanent rivers that supply drinking water; leaving them unprotected removes the federal check on discharges upstream of intakes [S3].

Wetlands are protected only if they have a continuous surface water connection visible to the naked eye, so wetlands that filter water and absorb floods but connect underground or only occasionally would lose protection, shifting cleanup and flood costs to the public [S3].

The 60-day default means a water is treated as unprotected whenever the Army Corps misses the deadline, and an 'unprotected' finding is binding indefinitely, locking in the narrower reading for that property [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a real, targeted benefit to agriculture, developers, and extractive industries by cutting federal permitting and pollution oversight on many waters. The cost is spread across the public: weaker protection for the streams and wetlands that feed drinking water sources and absorb floods, and federal water quality protection rolled back to only the most obviously permanent waters. On balance the gains are concentrated and the risks are diffuse.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which sent it to its water subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jaime Herrera Beutler introduced the bill on January 17, 2019, with Rep. Bob Gibbs as an original cosponsor, and it was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee [S1] [S3] [S5].
On February 7, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment; no further action is recorded for the rest of the 116th Congress [S5].
The bill drew only one cosponsor beyond the original sponsor list and never received a committee vote or floor action [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the 2015 clean water rule and the broader federal jurisdiction over streams and wetlands it targeted remained in place for the rest of that Congress, so communities that rely on those waters kept the stronger protections. The bill's intended beneficiaries — farmers, developers, and discharging industries — did not get the regulatory relief it offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Downstream communities kept existing water protections

for.name: Jaime Herrera Beutler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; recruited one cosponsor

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Peter DeFazio, D-OR), including its Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its water subcommittee on February 7, 2019 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: Support was exclusively Republican — a Republican sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, no Democratic support — but the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call shows how the parties lined up.

industries.note: The bill excludes ditches, drainage and irrigation systems, and prior converted cropland from federal protection and offers a fast binding determination that farm waters are unregulated. The gain comes from removing federal pollution oversight on waters that flow into rivers communities drink from.

Building near wetlands and small streams would require fewer federal permits and trigger less mitigation, cutting construction costs. The public bears the loss of wetlands that filter water and absorb floods.

Excluding ephemeral and intermittent streams, where much energy and mining activity occurs, would remove federal discharge permits and spill protections on those waters. Downstream water users absorb the resulting pollution risk.

industries.industry: Municipal water utilities and downstream water users
industries.note: With upstream tributaries and connecting wetlands excluded from the Clean Water Act, utilities and their customers face dirtier source water and higher treatment costs, with no compensating federal safeguard.
